title: Run JMESPath filters inside SQLite
description: Adds `jmespath/sqlite.py` so services that keep JSON documents in SQLite can filter them in the database instead of loading every row into Python. `where(condition, column='data')` compiles a filter condition (the part between `[?` and `]`) into a WHERE clause plus its parameters, for documents stored as JSON text in `column`. A row matches exactly when `jmespath.search('[?' + condition + ']', [document])` would keep its document. Supported: a comparison of a field or dotted path with a literal (string, number, `true`, `false` or `null`) on either side, `starts_with` and `ends_with` with a string literal, and `&&`, `||`, `!` and parentheses; a comparison only matches values of the literal's JSON type, and anything else raises `UnsupportedExpressionError`. Everything that comes from the expression reaches SQLite as a bound parameter, and table and column names are quoted, so any name works. `select(conn, table, condition, column='data')` runs the query on the caller's connection and returns the matching documents in rowid order. It only reads: committing or rolling back stays with the caller. Needs SQLite's JSON functions, built in since 3.38. Includes tests.

defects.summary: The JSON path is pasted into the SQL inside single quotes instead of being bound, so a field name with a quote breaks or rewrites the statement.
The GLOB pattern for starts_with and ends_with does not escape '[', so a literal bracket starts a character class and matches the wrong rows.
defects.corrected: text = ''.join('[%s]' % c if c in '*?[' else c
defects.defective: text = ''.join('[%s]' % c if c in '*?' else c

defects.summary: Identifiers are wrapped in double quotes without doubling the quotes inside them, so a table or column name containing a double quote breaks or rewrites the statement.
select wraps its query in 'with conn:', which commits whatever the caller had pending on the connection.
Swapping the sides of an ordering negates it instead of mirroring it, so `5` < n compiles to n >= 5.
True and false literals are classified as numbers because bool is checked after int, so on == `true` matches 1 and never matches true.

ceiling.summary: The double-quote check only looks at a plain field, so a key with a double quote inside a dotted path goes into the JSON path unescaped and reads another field (team."a\".\"b" reads team.a.b).
ceiling.corrected: if any('"' in key for key in keys):

decoys.anchor:
sql = 'IFNULL(%s IN %s AND %s %s ?, 0)' % (
                type_sql, types, value_sql, _OPERATORS[op])
decoys.why: The SQL is built with % formatting, but every piece is a constant from this module (the operator table, the type list, and json_type or json_extract with a ? placeholder); the value itself is bound.
Treating a missing field as null is JMESPath's own rule: a missing field evaluates to null, so field == `null` keeps documents without the field.
